Shade
SHAYD
n. (shelter from heat or light; comparative darkness caused by interception of the sun's rays)
Saxon sceadu, shadow, shade — the same root as shadow, from which shade is not sharply distinguished in older English. What casts a shade stands between a person and a heat that would otherwise fall directly upon him.

Biblical Definition

The Song of Ascents that is Psalm 121 spends its whole short length answering one question, where help comes from, and its middle verses give the answer its most physically vivid form: The LORD is thy keeper: the LORD is thy shade upon thy right hand. The image is of a pilgrim on the road up to Jerusalem, sun beating down through the heat of the day, and instead of a tree or a rock offering relief, it is the LORD Himself, positioned at the traveler's right hand, functioning as his personal shade against the very thing that would otherwise wear him down mile by mile.

The verses immediately following make the promise even more comprehensive: The sun shall not smite thee by day, nor the moon by night — shade against the sun's heat and, in the ancient world's own reckoning, protection from whatever harm the night and its moon were feared to bring as well. The Psalm never claims the pilgrim's road will be shortened or the heat removed from the world; it claims the LORD Himself will stand where the shade is needed, at exactly the hand where a traveler would naturally look for support. A psalm meant to be sung on pilgrimage gives its plainest comfort in the plainest possible image: not that the journey will be easy, but that the shade will not fail along the way.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): a place sheltered from the sun's rays; comparative obscurity or darkness caused by the interception of light.

expand to see more

SHADE, n. Comparative darkness caused by the interruption of the rays of light; a shelter from heat or glare.

KEEPER, n. One who guards, watches, or has the care and custody of a person or thing.

SMITE, v.t. To strike; to afflict, injure, or destroy, especially by a sudden or heavy blow.

PILGRIM, n. A wanderer or traveler, especially one journeying to a sacred place for religious purposes.

ASCENT, n. The act of rising or climbing; a way or path leading upward, as to a height or a holy place.

Key Scripture

Psa 121:5 — "The LORD is thy keeper: the LORD is thy shade upon thy right hand."

Psa 121:6 — "The sun shall not smite thee by day, nor the moon by night."

Psa 121:1 — "A Song of degrees. I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help."

Psa 121:8 — "The LORD shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in from this time forth, and even for evermore."

Modern Corruption

Shade is treated as passive relief from a difficulty already removed, when the Psalm names it as active, personal protection given precisely while the sun still beats and the journey still continues.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; shade still names shelter from heat or light. The principle worth recovering is what the Psalm does and does not promise. It does not say the sun's heat will be turned off or the road up to Jerusalem shortened; it says the LORD Himself will be positioned exactly where a traveler needs relief, at his right hand, for as long as the climb continues.

The Psalm's closing promise, that the LORD shall preserve a man's going out and coming in from this time forth and even for evermore, reveals that the shade of verse five is not a single moment's comfort but a standing arrangement for the whole of the pilgrimage, this journey and every one after it. A shade that only appeared once the heat had already passed would be no comfort at all; the Psalm's confidence rests on a shade given precisely at the hour of the sun's full strength.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tsel (H6738), shade, shadow, protection; the word applied to the LORD Himself in Psalm 121:5, and elsewhere to the shadow of His wings.

expand to see more

Hebrew tsel (H6738) — shade, shadow; the noun applied directly to the LORD as protector in Psalm 121:5.

Hebrew shamar (H8104) — to keep, to guard, to watch over; the verb behind “keeper,” repeated six times through this short Psalm.

Hebrew yamiyn (H3225) — the right hand; the position of honor and support where the LORD is said to stand.

Hebrew nakah (H5221) — to smite, to strike; the harm the sun and moon are here forbidden to inflict.

Hebrew ma'aleh (H4609, from the title Song of Degrees/Ascents) — a going up, an ascent; the pilgrimage setting of the whole Psalm.

Usage

"“The LORD is thy keeper: the LORD is thy shade upon thy right hand” — the Psalm's central image."

"“The sun shall not smite thee by day, nor the moon by night” — the shade's full, round-the-clock scope."

"“The LORD shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in” — the same shade extended over the whole of life."
